extraction.name: CoNLL-2003 Shared Task: Language-Independent Named Entity Recognition
extraction.description: A dataset for named entity recognition in English and German, containing training, development, and test files with annotations for four types of named entities: persons, locations, organizations and miscellaneous entities. The dataset includes annotated news articles with part-of-speech tags, chunk tags, and named entity tags.
extraction.creator: Erik F. Tjong Kim Sang and Fien De Meulder, CNTS - Language Technology Group, University of Antwerp
extraction.rai:dataCollection: English data was taken from Reuters news stories between August 1996 and August 1997. German data was extracted from the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundshau from articles written in one week at the end of August 1992.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: English data from Reuters Corpus (Reuters news stories August 1996 - August 1997). German data from ECI Multilingual Text Corpus (Frankfurter Rundshau newspaper).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: English: August 1996 - December 1996 for annotated data, September 1996 for raw data. German: End of August 1992 for annotated data, September - December 1992 for raw data.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The English data was tagged and chunked by the memory-based MBT tagger. The German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by the decision tree tagger Treetagger. Two basic language-specific tokenizers were created for this shared task. For all data, a tokenizer, part-of-speech tagger, and a chunker were applied to the raw data.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, and chunking were applied to raw data. English data was tagged and chunked by memory-based MBT tagger. German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by decision tree tagger Treetagger.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Named entity tagging was done by hand at the University of Antwerp, mostly following MUC conventions. An IOB tagging scheme was used with tags for persons (PER), organizations (ORG), locations (LOC) and miscellaneous names (MISC). Named entities are non-recursive and non-overlapping.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The tagging scheme is the IOB scheme originally put forward by Ramshaw and Marcus (1995). Named entities are assumed to be non-recursive and non-overlapping. When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated. Words tagged with O are outside of named entities and the I-XXX tag is used for words inside a named entity of type XXX. Whenever two entities of type XXX are immediately next to each other, the first word of the second entity will be tagged B-XXX in order to show that it starts another entity.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: MBT tagger for English (part-of-speech tagging and chunking), Treetagger for German (lemmatization, tagging and chunking)
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset contains names of persons as one of the four entity types being annotated.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development (parameter tuning), and testing of named entity recognition systems. The learning methods were trained with the training data. The development data could be used for tuning the parameters of the learning methods. When the best parameters were found, the method could be trained on the training data and tested on the test data.

name.evidence: We describe the CoNLL-2003 shared task: language-independent named entity recognition.

description.evidence: The CoNLL-2003 named entity data consists of eight files covering two languages: English and German. For each of the languages there is a training file, a development file, a test file and a large file with unannotated data.

url.evidence: Data files (except the words) can be found on http://lcg-www.uia.ac.be/conll2003/ner/

creator.evidence: Erik F. Tjong Kim Sang and Fien De Meulder, CNTS - Language Technology Group, University of Antwerp

inLanguage.evidence: The CoNLL-2003 named entity data consists of eight files covering two languages: English and German

isLiveDataset.evidence: For the training and development set, ten days' worth of data were taken from the files representing the end of August 1996. For the test set, the texts were from December 1996.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: The English data was taken from the Reuters Corpus. This corpus consists of Reuters news stories between August 1996 and August 1997. The text for the German data was taken from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus. The portion of data that was used for this task, was extracted from the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundshau.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: The English data was taken from the Reuters Corpus. The text for the German data was taken from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The English data was taken from the Reuters Corpus. This corpus consists of Reuters news stories between August 1996 and August 1997. The text for the German data was taken from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus. This corpus consists of texts in many languages. The portion of data that was used for this task, was extracted from the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundshau.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: For the training and development set, ten days' worth of data were taken from the files representing the end of August 1996. For the test set, the texts were from December 1996. The preprocessed raw data covers the month of September 1996. All three of the training, development and test sets were taken from articles written in one week at the end of August 1992. The raw data were taken from the months of September to December 1992.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The participants were given access to the corpus after some linguistic preprocessing had been done: for all data, a tokenizer, part-of-speech tagger, and a chunker were applied to the raw data. We created two basic language-specific tokenizers for this shared task. The English data was tagged and chunked by the memory-based MBT tagger (Daelemans et al., 2002). The German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by the decision tree tagger Treetagger (Schmid, 1995).

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Named entity tagging of English and German training, development, and test data, was done by hand at the University of Antwerp. Mostly, MUC conventions were followed (Chinchor et al., 1999). An extra named entity category called MISC was added to denote all names which are not already in the other categories. This tagging scheme is the IOB scheme originally put forward by Ramshaw and Marcus (1995). We assume that named entities are non-recursive and non-overlapping.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: The English data was tagged and chunked by the memory-based MBT tagger (Daelemans et al., 2002). The German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by the decision tree tagger Treetagger (Schmid, 1995).

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: We will concentrate on four types of named entities: persons, locations, organizations and names of miscellaneous entities that do not belong to the previous three groups.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: The learning methods were trained with the training data. The development data could be used for tuning the parameters of the learning methods. The challenge of this year's shared task was to incorporate the unannotated data in the learning process in one way or another. When the best parameters were found, the method could be trained on the training data and tested on the test data.
